question: Where is the industry heading on fee structures and pricing transparency?

claims.text: Uneven pressure, via transparency and unbundling rather than lower rates: a research piece ("Can advisory fees survive the collapse of planning costs?", published 2026-04-08) says it expects repricing where clients see no differentiation, such as basic tax projections. It calls the fear of an immediate, industry-wide fee freefall "likely overstated". It cites fee rates for relationships of more than $1 million staying at about 104 basis points since 2019, and says fee pressure will show up as "demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points."

Open to evolving pricing if clients and the market move: on Raymond James's fiscal 1Q26 call (period ending 2026-03-31, published 2026-04-22), the CEO said the aim is a "profitable and competitive and fair pricing structure". He said the firm would be "flexible and open to evolving" if the industry moves on competitive pressures and client preferences, and that it reviews pricing, fees and payout on an ongoing basis.

Continued price competition, flagged as a risk by the firms: Raymond James's 10-K (period 2025-09-30, published 2025-11-25) says regulatory requirements have produced greater price transparency in fixed income and equity markets, leading to price competition and lower trading margins. It says it believes pricing pressures will continue as some competitors seek share by cutting fees, commissions or margins. Schwab's 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) says it monitors competitors' pricing and adjusts advisory fees, fund expense ratios and commission rates. It says reduced commissions or lower expense ratios could affect its results.

Product-level fee compression: Edward Jones's 2025 10-K (published 2026-03-13) estimates about 20%, 21% and 22% of total revenue came from mutual fund and insurance products in 2025, 2024 and 2023. It cites "ongoing fee compression" across the mutual fund industry and says continued changes in industry fee structures or further compression of management or distribution fees could materially affect results.

New platform-level fees (trade press, indicative only): a trade article published 2026-09-29 reports a Merrill "support fee" on asset managers, capped at 10 basis points. It says sources attribute platform tolls at large distributors directly or indirectly to the zeroing out of commissions. It also says sources put Merrill's fee-based program pricing at typically 1.00% to 1.40% and as high as 1.75%, "comparable to RIAs pricing". These are sources' figures, not Merrill disclosures.

Transparency as an advisor differentiator (vendor research): a Wealthtender piece (published 2025-08-13) says many advisors avoid discussing fees upfront, creating an opportunity for transparent advisors. It recommends website fee pages, discussing pricing in the first 10 minutes of a first call, and written fee estimates after initial meetings.

What firms disclose on fee structures today (Form ADV brochures): Raymond James's Wealth Advisory Services brochure (published 2026-09-14) states planning fees as hourly (generally up to $400 per hour) or flat. It states investment consulting fees as hourly, flat or a percentage of assets not to exceed 2.25% annually. It notes some legacy clients pay under older schedules and that clients may pay more or less than at another firm. Edward Jones's brochure (published 2026-03-27) says Program Fee and Platform Fee rates are set by grouping related accounts into a Pricing Group, and it discloses group members on request. Merrill's brochure (published 2026-10-30) says compensation arrangements on certain products create a financial incentive for an advisor to recommend them. Merrill's press release (2026-09-15) says its new optional TET and DCA services carry no additional IAP Program Fees.

Regulatory focus on fees that clients cannot see: Morgan Stanley's 2026 ADV (published 2026-11-04) describes a 2020 SEC settlement order. The SEC found that from October 2012 through June 2017, MSWM gave misleading information about wrap programs, and some clients paid transaction-based charges "not visible to them".

gaps.what: No source in the evidence gives an industry-wide forecast of fee structures or a regulatory timetable for fee-transparency rules. The positions above are individual firm statements, research and trade press, not a consensus.
gaps.suggested_source: Industry fee surveys (for example advisory fee benchmarking studies), SEC/FINRA rulemaking releases, and firm investor-day materials on pricing
